newsitem.title: FRANCE: France changes government just when EMU fragile.
newsitem.headline: France changes government just when EMU fragile.

text.p: Victory by the Socialist-led opposition in Sunday's parliamentary election will give France a change of government just as Europe's plans for a single currency in 1999 are looking fragile.

But analysts said the Socialists, though likely to revive debate about what the continent wants out of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), are not expected to do anything which might put the project at risk.

The party has said it supports EMU, but with conditions, including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty, early membership for Italy and Spain and a European "economic government" to co-ordinate policies inside the euro zone.

Party leader Lionel Jospin, in what is probably the party's most controversial stance on Europe, has also said he does not feel bound to respect the "stability pact" agreed last year to limit budget deficits after the launch of a single currency.
Analysts say, however, that they do not believe that the Socialist Party, which negotiated Maastricht under the late President Francois Mitterrand, would block EMU if its demands are not met.
Jospin has said the party's conditions for supporting the euro are not "take it or leave it" conditions, but rather the basis for discussion with France's partners.
Confirming a first-round lead, the opposition Socialists beat the ruling centre-right in Sunday's runoff, according to early projections.

They will now share power with President Jacques Chirac, who ironically had called the election almost a year early to give his centre-right allies in government a stronger hand in the run-up to a single currency.
Chirac, who as president will retain ultimate responsibility for foreign policy, has repeatedly stressed his commitment to launching a single currency.
Economists say the new Socialist government is likely to back him up, seeking initially to calm things down in Europe and establish its credibility in financial markets.

Of all countries involved in the single currency plans, France may have the most to lose from a delay, after years of painful austerity policies meant to lead it to monetary marriage with Germany, its main postwar ally.
The new government takes power just as a row in Germany over a plan to revalue central bank gold to bolster public finances has revived speculation of a delay to the project.
The Bundesbank took the unusual step this weekend of issuing a statement saying its president, Hans Tietmeyer, had not suggested a delay.
The German weekly Der Spiegel had said Tietmeyer raised the possibility of a Franco-German initiative to put off EMU.

But while seeking to avoid adding fuel to the fire, France's new government is likely to try to shift the monetary union debate towards a more political vision of Europe's future -- a vision it shared with the centre-right, but which the outgoing government was unable to impose on France's partners.
The difference with the outgoing government is likely to be one of tone rather than substance.

While the previous government kept deliberately low-key about France's demands to avoid upsetting German public opinion -- hoping to win its case instead behind the scenes -- the Socialists have insisted it did not fight hard enough.

"If we have to live through a moment of high tension, and insist our demands are taken into consideration, we will do it," Henri Nallet, a former minister and specialist on Europe, told Reuters early in the campaign.

The Socialists are nonetheless expected to follow policies of sound financial management which would prevent the budget deficit from drifting too far beyond the three percent of gross domestic product ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty.
